Abstract In the rice genome, the SWEET gene family contains 21 homologous members, but the role of some of them
in rice growth and development is still unknown. The function of the sugar transporter OsSWEET1b protein in rice was
identified in this research. Expression analysis showed that the expression levels of OsSWEET1b in leaves were higher than
that in other tissues. The hexose transport experiment confirmed that OsSWEET1b has glucose and galactose transporter
activity in yeast. Subcellular localization indicates that OsSWEET1b protein was targeted to the plasma membrane and
BiFC analysis showed that OsSWEET1b interacts with itself to form homodimers. Functional analysis demonstrated that the
ossweet1b mutant plants were have reduced the sucrose, glucose, fructose, starch and galactose contents, and induced carbon
starvation-related gene expression, which might lead to carbon starvation in leaves at filling stage. The ossweet1b knockout
plants showed decreased chlorophyll content and antioxidant enzyme activity, and increased ROS accumulation in leaves,
leading to leaf cell death and premature senescence phenotype at filling stage. In ossweet1b mutants, the leaf senescence-
related gene expression levels were increased and the abundance of photosynthesis-related proteins was decreased. Loss
of OsSWEET1b were afected the starch, sucrose metabolism and carbon fixation in photosynthetic organelles pathway by
RNA-seq analysis. The destruction of OsSWEET1b function will cause sugar starvation, decreased photosynthesis and leaf
senescence, which leading to reduced rice yield. Collectively, our results suggest that the OsSWEET1b plays a key role in
rice leaves carbohydrate metabolism and leaf senescence.

of assimilates between diferent cells, tissues or organs were
requiring transporters protein in various plants. Transporters
are involved in transporting assimilates from source tissues
through the phloem to diferent sink tissues and influence
the plants growth and development (Chen et al. 2015a). In
plants, assimilates are transported in form the sugar, espe-
cially sucrose (Pommerrenig et al. 2007).

Two important sugar transporter families related to sugar
transport in diferent plants, namely sucrose transporters
(SUTs or SUCs) and sugars will eventually be exported
transporters (SWEETs) family proteins (Eom et al. 2015;
Garg and Kühn 2022). It’s report that sucrose transporters
have the ability to transport hexose or sucrose in various
plants. In Arabidopsis, the atsuc2 mutant exhibits reduced
sucrose transport in the phloem, resulting in excessive starch
accumulation in leaves, stunted growth, and reduced fertility
(Gong et al. 2015). In the atsuc4 mutant, accumulates higher
sucrose content in shoots compared to the WT but lower
sucrose levels in the roots, leading to altered growth (Gong
et al. 2015). In maize, ZmSUT1 gene mutation causes high
sugar content in leaves, displaying leaf chlorosis and stunted
growth (Baker et al. 2016). In rice, OsSUTs family proteins
contain five members, with OsSUT2 localized to the tono-
plast membrane, while the other four members are located
on the plasma membrane (Aoki et al. 2003). OsSUT1 is
essential for seed germination and seedling growth in rice
(Scofield et al. 2007). The hexose and sucrose content was
significantly increased in the ossut2 mutant compared to the
WT, leading to sugar excessive accumulation and growth
retardation (Eom et al. 2011).
SWEET proteins are responsible for the transport of sucrose
or hexose or fructose providing carbohydrates to various tis-
sues in plants (Chen et al. 2015b). In plants, SWEETs protein
can be divided into four clades by phylogenetic tree analysis.
Among them, in Arabidopsis thaliana, clade I and II mem-
bers were mainly responsible for hexose transport, clade III
members were sucrose transport, and clade IV members
were likely fructose transport (Wen et al. 2022; Eom et al.
2015). For example, clade III members AtSWEET11 and
AtSWEET12 have the function of sucrose transport based on
previous study (Gebauer et al. 2017). Although single mutants
for AtSWEET11 and AtSWEET12 do not exhibit any obvious
phenotypic changes, the double mutant atsweet11/atsweet12
shows increased starch content in leaves and enhanced dis-
ease resistance (Gebauer et al. 2017). The clade IV member
AtSWEET16 is located to the tonoplast and transports sucrose
and hexose like glucose and fructose (Klemens et al. 2013).
Overexpression of AtSWEET16 significantly alters leaf sugar
content, improves germination, and enhances freezing toler-
ance (Klemens et al. 2013). In crops, some SWEETs protein
was involved in the transport of assimilates from source to
sink, which was crucial for crop yields. For instance, in soy-
bean, GmSWEET15 is involved in sugar transport from the
endosperm to the embryo and is crucial for soybean embryo
development (Wang et al. 2019a, b). Loss of GmSWEET15
function results in reduced sugar content in the developing
embryo and a decreased seed-setting rate (Wang et al. 2019a,
b). In maize, ZmSWEET13 functions as a key transporter
for sucrose eflux into the apoplasm, and the zmsweet13abc
triple-knockout mutant displays excessive sugar accumulation,
reduced growth, and leaf chlorosis phenotype (Bezrutczyk
In rice, the OsSWEETs protein family consists of 21 mem-
bers (Yuan et al. 2014). OsSWEET4 is highly expressed at the
base of spikelet and is involved in endosperm basal hexose
transport (Sosso et al. 2015). OsSWEET5 transports galactose
and overexpression of OsSWEET5 increases hexose content in
leaves but leads to slow growth and premature senescence in
seedlings (Zhou et al. 2014). OsSWEET11, OsSWEET14, and
OsSWEET15 have been implicated in rice grain filling (Fei
et al. 2021; Ma et al. 2017; Yang et al. 2018). The ossweet11
mutant exhibits a 30% reduction in grain weight compared to
the WT, while the ossweet14 and ossweet15 mutants do not
show a grain weight phenotype. However, double mutants,
such as ossweet11-ossweet14 or ossweet11-ossweet15, display
a significant reduction in grain weight compared to ossweet11
mutants (Fei et al. 2021; Yang et al. 2018). OsSWEET1b
belongs to a subfamily that is diferent from OsSWEET4,
OsSWEET5, OsSWEET11, OsSWEET14, and OsSWEET15
(Yuan et al. 2014). Therefore, SWEETs protein plays an
important role in plant growth, stress tolerance, source to sink
sugar transport, and grain development. But the functions
of many OsSWEETs protein members in rice were remain
unclear and need to further research.
In this study, we characterized the OsSWEETs protein
member OsSWEET1b functions in rice. OsSWEET1b have
glucose and galactose transporter activity in yeast. It is
revealed that OsSWEET1b is predominantly expressed in
leaves and is localized to the plasma membrane. The expres-
sion and protein abundance of the photosynthesis-related
gene are reduced in ossweet1b-1 and ossweet1b-2 mutant
compared to WT plants. As a result, the mutants showed
leaf premature senescence phenotype during the grain-filling
stage, reduced grain weight and decreased seed setting at
mature stage. The ossweet1b-1 and ossweet1b-2 mutant were
reducing the sucrose, glucose, fructose, galactose and starch
contents in leaves, which likely leads to sugar starvation and
premature leaf senescence phenotypic. In conclusion, OsS-
WEET1b plays an important role in regulating rice leaves
carbohydrate metabolism and rice yields.

RNA‑seq analysis
The WT and ossweet1b-1 mutant leaves total RNA were
isolated at the filling stage, respectively. Approximately 6 μg
of total RNA from each sample was used to build the RNA-
seq libraries. The cDNA was then generated with random
hexamer primers and sequenced using Illumina HiSeq 2000
sequencing platform technology. Raw reads were processed
by removing adapter reads and low-quality date, and the
clean reads were mapping to the reference genome (ttp://
rice.plantbiology.msu.edu/index.shtml). The expression
level of gene was obtained and normalized to FPKM (frag-
ments per kilobase of transcript per million mapped reads)
(Li and Dewey 2011). In total, 40 and 44 million reads were
obtained from the WT and mutant plants, respectively,
which yielded 10,261 diferentially expressed genes (DEGs).
DEGs were defined as |Log FC|> 1.0. Next, we performed
Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and
Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analysis for DEGs (Bray et al.

RNA sequencing analysis of ossweet1b‑1 mutant
Transcriptome sequencing was performed on the WT and
ossweet1b-1 mutant leaves during the filling stage. In
total, 10,261 diferentially expressed genes (DEGs) were
identified, among of them 4517 showing significance
decrease and 5744 genes exhibiting significance increase
in the ossweet1b-1 mutant compared to the WT (Fig. 6a).
For instance, senescence-related genes including stay-
green (OsSGR), pectin methylesterase (OsPME), alkaline
α-galactosidase (Osh69) and OwWRKY72 were dramatically
upregulated in ossweet1b-1 mutant (Fig. 6b). GO enrichment
analysis indicated that the DEGs were involved in metabolic
process, carbohydrate binding, carbohydrate metabolic
processes and transporter activity (Fig. S5). For example,
nutrient transport-related genes included peptide transporter
2 (OsPTR2), peptide transporter 4 (OsPTR4), peptide trans-
porter 5 (OsPTR5), peptide transporter 6 (OsPTR6), peptide
transporter 9 (OsPTR9), lysine-histidine-type transporter
1 (OsLHT1) and ammonium transporter 2;1 (OsAMT2;1)
expression levels were significantly increased compare with
WT (Fig. 6c). These results suggest that OsSWEET1b muta-

mutant compared to the WT. Phylogenetic analysis showed
that SWEET1b can be divided into monocotyledonous and
dicotyledonous groups in various plants (Fig. S6). Therefore,

be more conserved in monocotyledons.

obvious at the filling stage, and this phase has significant
changes in the point source-sink relationship (Kumar et al.

the mutant, the expression levels of sugar synthesis-related

increased. This is consistent with the results of reduced
sugar content in the mutants. During the filling stage, nutri-

of sugar content in ossweet1b mutant may accelerate leaf
senescence process.

according to previous studies. By knocking out
GmSWEET15 was resulted in lower seed setting in soy-

was decreased by 30% and 70%, respectively (Fei et al.

depending on translocation of photosynthetic substances

show sugar starvation and premature leaf senescence at
the grain filling stage. Although the nutriment transport-
related genes were upregulation in the mutants leaves than
WT. But the ossweet1b mutant 1000-grain weight and seed
setting was reduced by about 15% and 33%, respectively.

in ossweet1b mutants than WT. This may be because the
ossweet1b mutants leaves lost source capacity in the filling
stage and were not able to produce enough photo-assimi-

In summary, we identified the function of OsSWEET1b,
which is diferent from most of the previously reported func-
tions of SWEET in rice. The majority of SWEET gene muta-
tions can cause sugar accumulation, which leading to leaf
senescence phenotype and influence crop yield. In this study,
we suggested that loss of OsSWEET1b function can lead to
sugar starvation and cause leaf senescence during the grain
filling stage, which afects rice yield. The OsSWEET1b
belongs to a diferent subfamily from previously reported
OsSWEET proteins including OsSWEET4, OsSWEET5,
OsSWEET11 and so on in rice, and their functions may be
diferentiated. These results will contribute to a better under-

and development.

obvious at the filling stage, and this phase has significant
changes in the point source-sink relationship (Kumar et al.
2019). Thus, the OsSWEET1b activity may be mediating
the shifts in the source-sink relationship. The appearance
of ossweet1b mutant phenotype in filling stage may also be
due to the reduced functional complementarity of the OsS-
WEET1b homolog. For example, the expression of OsS-
WEET2b, OsSWEET3b, OsSWEET13 and OsSWEET16 was
reduced in ossweet1b mutants. On the other hand, RNA-seq
analysis demonstrated that the expression of sugar metabo-
lism-related genes greatly changed in the mutant plants. In
the mutant, the expression levels of sugar synthesis-related
genes were inhibited, but the degradation-related genes was
increased. This is consistent with the results of reduced
sugar content in the mutants. During the filling stage, nutri-
ents from leaves are transferred to grains. The reduction
of sugar content in ossweet1b mutant may accelerate leaf
senescence process.
The SWEET gene was influence crop yield traits
according to previous studies. By knocking out
GmSWEET15 was resulted in lower seed setting in soy-
bean (Wang et al. 2019a, b). In the ossweet11 mutant and
ossweet11;14 double rice mutants, the 1000-grain weight
was decreased by 30% and 70%, respectively (Fei et al.
2021; Yang et  al. 2018). The grains yield was mainly
depending on translocation of photosynthetic substances
from leaves to grains. In this study, ossweet1b mutants
show sugar starvation and premature leaf senescence at
the grain filling stage. Although the nutriment transport-
related genes were upregulation in the mutants leaves than
WT. But the ossweet1b mutant 1000-grain weight and seed
setting was reduced by about 15% and 33%, respectively.
And the yield per plant reduced by approximately 62%
in ossweet1b mutants than WT. This may be because the
ossweet1b mutants leaves lost source capacity in the filling
stage and were not able to produce enough photo-assimi-
lates for translocation into grains.
In summary, we identified the function of OsSWEET1b,
which is diferent from most of the previously reported func-
tions of SWEET in rice. The majority of SWEET gene muta-
tions can cause sugar accumulation, which leading to leaf
senescence phenotype and influence crop yield. In this study,
we suggested that loss of OsSWEET1b function can lead to
sugar starvation and cause leaf senescence during the grain
filling stage, which afects rice yield. The OsSWEET1b
belongs to a diferent subfamily from previously reported
OsSWEET proteins including OsSWEET4, OsSWEET5,
OsSWEET11 and so on in rice, and their functions may be
diferentiated. These results will contribute to a better under-
standing the role of OsSWEET1b function in rice growth
and development.
